newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. labour boss hits firms over worker rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labour boss hits firms over worker rights.

text.p: U.S. labour leader John Sweeney warned corporate executives on Friday that the chase after profits at the expense of worker salaries and social protection would bring a destructive worldwide backlash.

And he told the Davos World Economic Forum that experience in the United States showed that companies which had followed the path of "downsizing" their work force and slashing benefits ended up in worse shape than they had started.

Debate at the annual meeting of business and political leaders seemed based on an assumption of a contradiction between competitiveness and measures that made working families secure such as good wages, health care and strong unions, he said.
"This assumption may be the fastest growing export of what is called the U.S. model," said Sweeney, president of the AFL-CIO labour grouping.
"But I am here to warn you. With all due respect, it is a highly costly, very toxic export, dangerous to the health and welfare of working people and national economies across the world," he said.

Examples of what could happen were the strife that has been rocking South Korea over a new labour law, the popular support in France for public service workers resisting government spending cuts, and the recent general strike in Argentina.

"In the United States, we hear much about the American job machine. Worker productivity is up. Stock prices are soaring. Executive salaries are sky-rocketing," said Sweeney, one of several labour leaders attending the Forum.
"But most working people are working longer and harder just to make ends meet. We are growing apart," he declared.
"This is the result of corporate choices, not economic laws. Too many companies rewarded by government incentives have taken the low road in international competition.

"They are cutting their workforces, their wages and their benefits. They are fighting against working people and their unions. They scour the globe is search of places where working people have low wages and no rights."

Sweeney's blunt challenge to corporate chiefs, who have been the backbone of the Forum since it was launched in 1971, is expected to be reinforced at a session next Monday when other worker leaders join a formal debate on "the agenda for labour."

These include Bill Jordan, general secretary of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), Fritz Verzetnitsch of Austria who is president of the European Trade Union Confederation, and union chiefs from France, Germany and South Africa.
Officials with some of them hail the organisers' decision to hold the session as a sign that their message is beginning to have an effect.

"New forms of dialogue at the world level need to be established to get to grips with the problems of social sustainability into the next century," said a statement from the Geneva-based white collar global union federation FIET.

Sweeney said that in the 25 years after World War Two, rich and poor people benefited from a set of common values that assumed working people were entitled to a fair share of the wealth they produced and pushed up living standards all round.

But the reaction in the United States to the change, he said, was also "feeding an ugly backlash, already in evidence.... a surly nationalism, a destructive discord, turning people one against the other," he declared.
